topic.subject: science
topic.title: Electric circuits
topic.scope: cell, bulb, switch, closed and open circuits, conductors and insulators, series connection of cells

misconceptions.statement: Electricity flows from the battery to the bulb through a single wire and stops there.
misconceptions.why: Students see a single wire in some diagrams or think of electricity like water from a tap.
misconceptions.fix: Electricity must return to the source; it requires a complete, unbroken loop from one terminal to the other.

probe.question: If you connect one wire from the positive terminal of a cell to the tip of a bulb, will it glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the electricity reaches the bulb.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one connection is needed for effect
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's research on children's ideas

misconceptions.statement: The bulb consumes electricity, so less current returns to the battery than what left it.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse energy (which is transformed) with current (which is conserved).
misconceptions.fix: The amount of current flowing into the bulb is exactly equal to the amount flowing out of it.

probe.question: Compare the current in the wire before the bulb and the wire after the bulb.
probe.wrong_answer: The current after the bulb is less because the bulb used it.

misconceptions.root_belief: electricity is a substance that gets used up

misconceptions.statement: Electricity travels from both terminals of the battery and meets at the bulb to make it light up.
misconceptions.why: The symmetrical appearance of circuits leads students to believe in a 'clashing' model.
misconceptions.fix: Current flows in one continuous direction around the loop, from positive to negative.

probe.question: How does electricity move from a cell to a bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: It comes from both sides and crashes in the bulb.

misconceptions.root_belief: two opposing forces meet to create an effect

misconceptions.statement: The bulb only has one terminal at the bottom tip.
misconceptions.why: The metal casing of the bulb is often mistaken for a holder rather than a functional terminal.
misconceptions.fix: An electric bulb has two terminals: the metal tip at the base and the metal casing around the base.

probe.question: Where should the two wires from a cell be connected to a bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: Both wires should touch the bottom tip of the bulb.

misconceptions.root_belief: only the most prominent part is functional

misconceptions.statement: All non-metal materials are perfect insulators and can never conduct electricity.
misconceptions.why: Textbooks emphasize metals as conductors, leading to overgeneralization about non-metals like graphite or impure water.
misconceptions.fix: While most non-metals are insulators, some like graphite (pencil lead) and certain liquids can conduct electricity.

probe.question: Will a circuit work if you use a pencil lead (graphite) to bridge a gap?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because it is not a metal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category property applies to every member

misconceptions.statement: A switch stores electricity when it is in the OFF position.
misconceptions.why: Students use everyday language like 'storing' or 'stopping' and imagine the switch as a dam.
misconceptions.fix: A switch simply creates a gap in the circuit; it does not store any electricity.

probe.question: What happens to the electricity when the switch is turned off?
probe.wrong_answer: It stays inside the switch waiting to be released.

misconceptions.root_belief: stopping flow means accumulation at the barrier

misconceptions.statement: Two cells in a torch will work regardless of which way their ends are facing.
misconceptions.why: Students may not realize that the orientation of terminals determines the direction of potential.
misconceptions.fix: Cells must be connected in series with the positive terminal of one touching the negative terminal of the next.

probe.question: If you put two cells in a torch with both positive ends facing each other, will it light up?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, as long as there are two cells, it will work.

misconceptions.root_belief: quantity of components matters more than arrangement

misconceptions.statement: The glass of the bulb is what produces the light.
misconceptions.why: The glass is the largest and most visible part of the bulb that appears to glow.
misconceptions.fix: The light is produced by the thin wire inside called the filament when it becomes hot.

probe.question: Which part of the bulb actually glows?

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: Air is a good conductor because electricity travels through it during lightning.
misconceptions.why: Students observe lightning and conclude that air must always allow electricity to pass.
misconceptions.fix: Air is generally an insulator; lightning only occurs when the electrical pressure is extremely high.

probe.question: If there is a small gap between two wires in a circuit, will the bulb glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because electricity can travel through the air.

misconceptions.root_belief: extreme cases represent the normal state

misconceptions.statement: A battery is like a reservoir full of electricity that flows out like water.
misconceptions.why: The water-pipe analogy is often taken too literally by students.
misconceptions.fix: A battery is a source of energy that pushes charges already present in the wires.

probe.question: Where does the electricity come from when a circuit is closed?
probe.wrong_answer: It is stored inside the battery and flows out into the wires.

misconceptions.statement: A thicker wire will always make a bulb glow brighter than a thinner wire.
misconceptions.why: Students associate 'bigger' or 'thicker' with 'more power' or 'easier flow'.
misconceptions.fix: In simple Class 6 circuits, the thickness of short connecting wires does not visibly change the bulb's brightness.

probe.question: If you replace a thin copper wire with a very thick one, what happens to the bulb?
probe.wrong_answer: It will glow much brighter because more electricity can fit.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: A circuit is closed as long as the wires are touching the bulb anywhere on its surface.
misconceptions.why: Students do not realize that specific internal paths exist within the bulb.
misconceptions.fix: A circuit is only closed if the wires are connected to the two specific terminals of the bulb.

probe.question: If you touch both wires to the glass part of the bulb, will it glow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the wires are touching the bulb.

misconceptions.root_belief: contact with the whole is contact with the part
